newsitem.title: USA: Clinton orders probe into classified data on donor.
newsitem.headline: Clinton orders probe into classified data on donor.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday said the White House was looking into a report that classified information was improperly given to the Democratic Party so it could assess the background of a campaign donor.
The Washington Post reported on Tuesday that top-secret intelligence data was given to the Democratic National Committee regarding a Latvian business executive with alleged ties to organised crime.
As a result of the information, the donor, Grigori Loutchansky, was barred from a $25,000 per person fund-raising dinner that Clinton attended, the newspaper said.

Clinton said that White House legal counsel Charles Ruff "held a series of conversations, which at ... the present time, do not reveal any basis for believing that any sensitive information was improperly transmitted to the DNC."
"But because it's nonetheless a serious allegation, I met with my counsel ... about what next steps should be taken, to look into it further."
"But based on conversations so far, we have no basis to believe that it was done," said Clinton, during a joint news conference in the Rose Garden with Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien.
The newspaper said political operatives in the White House told the DNC that the National Security Agency was monitoring Loutchansky's international phone calls.
Loutchansky's firm, Nordex, was allegedly associated with Russian organised crime organisations, officials told the Post.

House of Representatives Intelligence Committee Chairman Porter Goss, a Florida Republican, said his panel was investigating the report. He also released a November 1996 letter he had sent to then White House chief of staff Leon Panetta seeking information on Loutchansky.

That letter specifically asked whether the intelligence community made any effort to withdraw a 1995 DNC fundraising invitation to Loutchansky. Goss asked for a response by Dec 6, 1996, but said he had yet to receive an answer.

"If this allegation proves true, and this disclosure actually took place, it constitutes a felony violation. I am very troubled by the implications for breaches of long-standing security controls at the White House," Goss said in a statement.
White House spokesman Barry Toiv said the National Security Council's standard practice was never to explain the basis for a recommendation on an individual.
The Post quoted a senior official as saying the incident underscored the "total politicization of all intelligence and White House operations."
"Anything and everything was done in the name of fund raising," the newspaper quoted the official as saying.

The Clinton administration has faced a barrage of recent allegations about improper fund raising, as well as reports of lax security that allowed a number of felons, drug dealers and other questionable characters to attend White House coffees and dinners.
Loutchansky now lives in Israel and is barred from entering the United States, Canada and Britain. His attorney, Thomas Spencer Jr., disputed reports of his client's ties to organised crime.
